Q24
Project Description #1 – Describe ONE project, effort, or service provided by the CHC.
In 2024, The Bell CHC & Bell Museum created a quarterly history education program collaboration where we co-sponsored two public
1-hour lunch-and-learns and made them available to county residents. Both sessions were hosted by the Bell County Museum, with
the first session highlighting County Historic Districts, which included city officials from Belton, Temple, Killeen, and Salado giving
presentations. Bartlett city staff did not present but attended. There were over 35 attendees for this inaugural event. Each city has
historic districts, and the session allowed many history and preservation enthusiasts to attend. Our second 2024 session was a Camp
Hood history with over 40 attendees. Straddling both Bell and Coryell Counties, the recently renamed Fort Cavzos has been a staple to
the region since World War II and served as an anchor for much of the 1950s-1960s growth in our area.

Q25
Project Description #2 – Describe ONE project, effort, or service provided by the CHC.
On November 14, the May 26, 1839 Battle of Bird's CreekBird heritage site was unveiled by a group of participants on the former
battlegrounds in the City of Temple. This was a culmination of an almost 2-year long project co-sponsored by the Bell County Historical
Commission and the City of Temple. To save this historic site, an ad hoc committee was formed, and the staff of the Community
Vitality Department of the City of Temple’s Planning Department took the lead in coordinating a plan to preserve and recreate the battle
through story. The committee comprised City, County, and State historical agencies, the Texas Ranger Hall of Fame & Museum, and
the Daughters of the Republic of Texas (DRT). The group coordinated with landowners WB Development and the builders DR Horton to
gain their support and create a long-lasting tribute to preserve and interpret a portion of the Comanche Hunting grounds and the site of
the Bird Creek Battle. The landowners gifted space for a previously obstructed centennial marker to be relocated on their property near
the edge of the ravine where Texas Ranger Captain John Bird and his men were pinned down. The builders graded the area, created a
parklet space in a portion of the battlefield, and built a sidewalk walking trail around the battlefield at their own expense. They
separated the battlefield from the housing with the addition of fencing and three stone seating benches. The City of Temple, working
with the Bell County Historical Commission, designed interpretive signage around the battlefield, telling the story of the events leading
up to the final engagement and the battle. The signage included photographs of periodic artifacts provided by the Texas Ranger Hall of
Fame & Museum and sketches of the battle scenes by local artist Susan Sterle. The City of Temple Parks & Recreation landscaped
the area, including hydro-seeding and additional trees for shade. In 2024, the Texas Historical Commission approved a historical
marker nomination, Commanche Hunting Grounds Battlefield, to be placed on the site sometime in the future. The DRT placed a
welcome sign at the entry to the site describing the significance of the legacy of the Republic and has approved a DRT medallion to be
placed alongside the centennial marker for Bird and his men. Protecting and interpreting this tangible historic place is a unique
attraction for the City of Temple and Bell County and will add a new cultural site to the region’s heritage tourism offerings.

Q26
Project Description #3 – Describe ONE project, effort, or service provided by the CHC.
In 2024, the Bell CHC embarked on a 6-month long project to update its Bell County Historical Resources Guide. This 35-page
pamphlet was a rewrite and update of an earlier 2001 edition with two major sections. The first is a listing of Federal, State, County,
and City agencies related to preserving history, including government agencies, non-profits, volunteer organizations, museums, and
other interested parties. It includes contact info, phone numbers, email addresses, websites, and historic photographs from county
activities interspersed across the booklet. The second section includes a bibliography created by local history enthusiast Patricia
Benoit. There is also a section on digital collections, online archives, and other useful information for those interested in county
history. It was created in part as a tribute to Bell County's 175th year, to be celebrated January 22, 2025.
